title: Why Relics Matter
description: The cult of saints, the grades of relics, and the bodies under altars and stupas

concepts.title: The Very Special Dead
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 155 to 160 CE a bishop was burned at Smyrna, and his community gathered his bones, "more precious than precious stones," laid them in a fitting place, and planned to meet there each year on the "birthday" of his martyrdom, the day he died. That account, the Martyrdom of Polycarp, is where Christian veneration of relics is first clearly documented. A relic (Latin reliquiae, "remains") is a physical trace of a holy person, whether a body, a bone, a scrap of clothing or an object they touched.

Walk out through the gate of a Roman city and you'd pass tombs lining the road, because Roman custom kept the dead outside city walls. Christians reversed that. In 386 Bishop Ambrose of Milan announced the discovery of the bodies of two martyrs, Gervasius and Protasius, had them carried in procession, and buried them beneath the altar of his new basilica. Augustine, then living in Milan, recorded the event in his Confessions.

The historian Peter Brown argued in The Cult of the Saints (1981) that bishops and the elite led this veneration. The older "two-tier" model, which he traced back to David Hume, had treated it as a superstition welling up from the uneducated and grudgingly tolerated by the clergy. The saints were, in Brown's phrase, "the very special dead." At their tombs heaven and earth were thought to meet, and the saint acted as a patron, a friend with influence at the court of God. The saint's praesentia (presence) and potentia (power) made a grave a place to seek healing, justice and protection. Brown's subject was the Latin West between about 250 and 600 CE, and his central claim, that relics were mainstream rather than marginal, reshaped the whole field.

concepts.title: First, Second and Third Class
concepts.contentHtml:
In 594 the Byzantine empress Constantina asked Pope Gregory the Great for the head of Saint Paul. Gregory refused, explaining that Roman custom forbade disturbing the saints' bodies. He offered cloths that had lain near the apostles' tombs, called brandea, and filings from the chains said to have bound Saint Peter instead. Gregory of Tours, writing in Gaul in the same period, describes pilgrims lowering cloths onto Peter's tomb and claiming they came up heavier, as if soaked with holiness.

Catholic devotion traditionally sorts relics into three grades, and the bone you might picture is only the first. A first-class relic is part of the saint's body, such as bone, hair, blood, or the whole corpse. A second-class relic is something the saint owned or used, like a garment, a book or an instrument of martyrdom. A third-class relic is any object touched to a first- or second-class relic, often a small square of cloth. The grades are a devotional convention rather than a fixed legal category, and the Vatican's 2017 instruction on relics speaks more simply of "significant" relics (a body or a substantial part of one) and lesser ones.

The logic was contagion. Holiness was thought to pass by touch, so a relic could be multiplied without dividing the body. Church law has long tried to keep money out of it. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) banned the sale of relics and their display outside a reliquary,1 and the current Code of Canon Law (1983) states that selling sacred relics is "absolutely forbidden."2

concepts.title: Bodies Under Altars, Ashes Under Stupas
concepts.contentHtml:
Burying martyrs beneath altars hardened into law. The Second Council of Nicaea (787), called mainly to restore the veneration of icons after Byzantine iconoclasm, ruled in its seventh canon that churches consecrated without relics must have them deposited,1 and that a bishop who consecrated a church without relics should be deposed. Orthodox priests still celebrate the liturgy on an antimension, a cloth with a relic sewn into it. Modern Catholic law is softer, calling relics under a fixed altar an "ancient tradition" to be preserved, though it isn't a strict condition.

Buddhism developed a relic culture centuries earlier. According to the Mahaparinibbana Sutta of the Pali canon, after the Buddha's cremation at Kusinara (Kushinagar), eight peoples and kings demanded his remains and nearly fought over them. A Brahmin named Dona divided the bones into eight shares. He kept the measuring vessel, and a latecomer clan received the embers, making ten monuments in all.2 A later legend, in the Ashokavadana, has the emperor Ashoka (3rd century BCE) redistribute the relics into 84,000 stupas.

Picture a solid dome built over relics, and you have a stupa. Pali commentaries sort shrines into bodily relics (saririka), things the Buddha used, such as his bowl or the Bodhi tree (paribhogika), and commemorative images (uddesika), a scheme close to the Christian grades. Archaeology touches the story too. In 1898 William Peppé opened a stupa at Piprahwa, near the Nepal border, and found an inscribed urn that many scholars read as naming relics of the Buddha of the Sakya clan, though the reading and date are debated.

title: Holy Theft
description: Why medieval writers boasted of stealing saints, from Alexandria to Bari

concepts.title: Furta Sacra: Theft as a Genre
concepts.contentHtml:
Between about 800 and 1100, monasteries and towns across western Europe produced proud accounts of how they had stolen their saints. The historian Patrick Geary studied these narratives in Furta Sacra: Thefts of Relics in the Central Middle Ages (1978). The Latin phrase means "sacred thefts," and Geary showed that they formed a recognizable genre within the translatio, the account of a relic's transfer, with stock episodes: a community in need, a daring journey, a secret raid on a tomb, miracles on the road, a joyful arrival.

Boasting of theft made sense because a saint was understood as a living person who could not be moved against his or her will. A successful theft proved that the saint consented, even wanted to leave a neglectful home for a more devoted one. Purchase, by contrast, looked mercenary and raised doubts about authenticity. Some thefts really happened; others were probably invented later to give an existing relic a grander past. Geary reads the texts as evidence of what communities needed to believe, not as reliable crime reports.

A real trade lay behind the stories. In the 820s a Roman deacon named Deusdona supplied bones from the catacombs to Frankish clients, and Einhard, Charlemagne's biographer, obtained the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter for his foundation at Seligenstadt through such dealings. The monks of Conques told how one of their brothers lived for about ten years at Agen, winning trust, before carrying off the body of the girl martyr Sainte Foy around 866. Her gold reliquary statue still stands at Conques.

concepts.title: Saint Mark and the Basket of Pork
concepts.contentHtml:
The most famous theft gave Venice its patron. According to the Translatio sancti Marci, in 828 two Venetian merchants, Buono da Malamocco and Rustico da Torcello, were in Alexandria, where the evangelist Mark was venerated as founder of the city's church. Hearing that his church was being stripped of materials, they persuaded its custodians, a priest named Theodore and a monk named Stauracius, to hand over the body. They carried it to their ship in a basket covered with pork, and the Muslim customs officers, recoiling from the meat, let it pass.

The oldest surviving version of the story dates from the eleventh century, two centuries after the event, though it probably drew on earlier writing. The pork episode is best read as tradition: vivid, plausible, and impossible to check. That Venice acquired a body it identified as Mark's around 828 is not in doubt; it was housed in a chapel beside the doge's palace, the ancestor of the Basilica of San Marco.

The relic was a political asset. Mark outranked Venice's earlier patron, the soldier-saint Theodore, and an evangelist founder strengthened the lagoon's church against the rival patriarchate of Aquileia. A legend recorded in the thirteenth century added that an angel had once greeted Mark on the lagoon with the words Pax tibi Marce evangelista meus ("Peace to you, Mark, my evangelist"), turning the theft into a homecoming. A thirteenth-century mosaic over the basilica's Porta di Sant'Alipio still shows the body being carried in.

concepts.title: Saint Nicholas Goes to Bari
concepts.contentHtml:
Saint Nicholas was a fourth-century bishop of Myra in Lycia, on the southern coast of modern Turkey (today's Demre). Almost nothing about his life is securely documented; the story of his secret gifts of dowry money to three poor girls, a root of his later role as Santa Claus, comes from later hagiography. His tomb at Myra was a major pilgrimage site.

In spring 1087 sailors and merchants from Bari, in southern Italy, sailed to Myra, reportedly racing a Venetian expedition with the same plan. The region had come under Seljuk Turkish control after the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071. Over the protests of the Greek monks guarding the church, the Barese broke open the tomb and took most of the bones, landing at Bari on 9 May 1087. The Barese accounts, by the cleric Nicephorus and by John the Archdeacon, present the raid as a rescue from Muslim hands; the monks of Myra saw a robbery. Pope Urban II placed the relics in the crypt of the new Basilica of San Nicola in 1089.

The Venetians took what remained at Myra during the First Crusade (1099 to 1100) and housed it at San Nicolò al Lido. Anatomical studies have found the Bari and Venice bones compatible with a single skeleton. Each year clergy at Bari still draw off a clear liquid called manna from the tomb; its source is unexplained, and moisture seeping into the low-lying crypt is a common natural suggestion. In 2017 a portion of the relics was lent to Moscow and St Petersburg, where well over a million Orthodox believers queued to venerate it.

title: Improbable Relics
description: Holy foreskins, enough cross to fill a ship, and the critics who laughed

concepts.title: The Holy Foreskins
concepts.contentHtml:
Christian doctrine holds that Christ rose and ascended bodily, which left little of his body behind. Churches nonetheless claimed his blood, tears, milk teeth and hair, and, because Luke's Gospel says he was circumcised on the eighth day, his foreskin. The Holy Prepuce (Latin praeputium) was claimed by more than a dozen churches across medieval Europe, sometimes at the same time; popular counts run higher.

The abbey of Charroux in Poitou said Charlemagne had given it the relic, a legend rather than a record. The papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum at the Lateran in Rome claimed one too, and Pope Innocent III, faced with the rival claims in the early thirteenth century, declined to rule on which was genuine. In 1856 a workman repairing the ruined abbey at Charroux reportedly found a reliquary hidden in a wall.

Calcata is a hill village north of Rome. Local tradition holds that a German soldier looted the Lateran relic during the Sack of Rome in 1527, was caught near Calcata, and hid it, and that it was found there years later. The village paraded it every 1 January, the Feast of the Circumcision. According to the journalist David Farley, a Vatican decree of 1900 threatened excommunication for anyone who wrote or spoke about the relic, and the feast itself was dropped from the general Roman calendar in the 1960s. In 1983 the parish priest announced that the relic had been stolen from his home. Whether thieves wanted its jeweled case or church authorities quietly removed it has never been established, and it has not resurfaced.

concepts.title: Enough Wood to Fill a Ship
concepts.contentHtml:
The cross of Christ became the most widespread relic in Christendom. The legend that Constantine's mother, the empress Helena, found it in Jerusalem appears first in Ambrose of Milan's funeral oration for Theodosius in 395, some seventy years after her visit to Palestine; Eusebius, who described that visit at the time, says nothing of a cross. Wood venerated as the cross was in Jerusalem by about 350, though, when Bishop Cyril remarked that fragments of it had already filled the world.

The pilgrim Egeria, visiting in the 380s, describes the Good Friday ceremony: the faithful filed past to kiss the wood while deacons stood guard, because someone was said to have once bitten off a piece and carried it away. Fragments spread through gifts, diplomacy and, after the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, plunder. Paulinus of Nola, around 403, answered the obvious objection in advance: the cross, he wrote, gave away pieces without growing smaller.

Skeptics did the arithmetic. John Calvin, in his Treatise on Relics (1543), wrote that if all the fragments were gathered together they would make a full load for a large ship. In 1870 the French architect Charles Rohault de Fleury, a Catholic answering such jibes, cataloged and measured the known fragments. He put their total at roughly 4 million cubic millimeters, against about 178 million for a cross of the size he assumed: on his figures the surviving relics came to only a small fraction of one cross. Both numbers rest on guesses about lost pieces and the cross's dimensions.

concepts.title: Mockers Inside and Outside the Church
concepts.contentHtml:
Doubt about relics did not begin with the Protestants. Around 1120 the Benedictine abbot Guibert of Nogent wrote On the Relics of the Saints, attacking the monks of Saint-Médard at Soissons for displaying what they said was a baby tooth of Christ. His argument was theological as well as practical: Christ's body rose whole, so claims to pieces of it were suspect. In the 1390s Chaucer gave his Pardoner a glass full of "pigges bones" to pass off as saints' remains.

The Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus made the mockery literary. His Praise of Folly (1511) laughed at people who prayed to a different saint for every ailment, and his colloquy A Pilgrimage for Religion's Sake (1526) drew on his own visits to Walsingham and Canterbury. Its speakers joke that the Virgin left so much milk on earth that one woman with one child could hardly have produced it, and that the fragments of the cross would fill a merchant ship. At Canterbury a companion modeled on the scholar John Colet treats the relics of Thomas Becket with open disgust. Erasmus stayed a Catholic and aimed his mockery at credulity and profit.

Calvin went further. His 1543 treatise proposed a full inventory of Europe's relics, confident that duplicated bodies and impossible objects would discredit the whole system. Catholic reform answered in its own way: the Council of Trent (1563) defended the veneration of relics while ordering bishops to root out superstition and "filthy lucre" in their cult.

title: The Buddha's Tooth
description: A canine tooth that made kings, outlived a Portuguese bonfire, and leads a procession

concepts.title: From Kalinga to Lanka
concepts.contentHtml:
Sri Lankan Buddhist chronicles, above all the Pali Dathavamsa ("Chronicle of the Tooth," composed in the thirteenth century from an older Sinhala work), tell the relic's origin story. At the Buddha's cremation an elder named Khema took the left canine tooth from the pyre and gave it to the king of Kalinga, on India's east coast, who enshrined it at Dantapura, "Tooth City." Generations later, when war threatened it, Princess Hemamala and her husband Prince Dantha are said to have smuggled it to Sri Lanka hidden in her hair, arriving in the reign of King Sirimeghavanna in the early fourth century CE.

That account is tradition, written down long after the events. Independent evidence begins with the Chinese monk Faxian, who stayed in Anuradhapura around 410 to 412 CE and described the tooth being carried in a great annual procession to the Abhayagiri monastery, along a route swept and decorated for the occasion. By then it was firmly a royal relic.

In Sri Lankan political tradition, whoever held the tooth had the right to rule, and the relic moved with the capital: from Anuradhapura to Polonnaruwa, then to Dambadeniya, Yapahuwa, Kurunegala, Gampola, Kotte and finally Kandy. Kings built a temple for it, a Dalada Maligawa, near each palace. The chronicles record that in the late thirteenth century a South Indian Pandyan army carried the tooth off from Yapahuwa and that a Sri Lankan king recovered it by negotiation.

concepts.title: The Portuguese Bonfire of 1561
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1560 a Portuguese expedition led by the viceroy of India, Dom Constantino de Bragança, attacked the kingdom of Jaffna in northern Sri Lanka and seized a tooth relic that had been carried there. The Portuguese chroniclers Diogo do Couto and João de Barros tell what followed. Bayinnaung, king of Pegu in Burma, offered an enormous ransom for it. Some officials in Goa wanted to accept; the archbishop, Gaspar de Leão Pereira, and the clergy insisted that a Christian state could not sell an idol. In 1561 the tooth was publicly ground in a mortar and burned, and its ashes were thrown into the water.

Sri Lankan Buddhists have never accepted that this was the real relic. The tradition preserved at Kandy holds that the authentic tooth had been hidden for safety at the Delgamuwa temple near Ratnapura, concealed in a grinding stone, and that the Portuguese destroyed a replica. The picture was muddier still: according to Portuguese and Burmese sources, within a few years another "true" tooth was presented to Bayinnaung by a Sri Lankan ruler, and by the 1590s the new kingdom of Kandy enshrined its own.

Historians cannot settle which, if any, of these was the tooth Faxian saw, because the evidence is chronicles written by interested parties on every side. The Kandy relic's claim rests on continuous custody as told in Buddhist tradition; the Portuguese claim rests on their own triumphant reports.

concepts.title: Kandy and the Esala Perahera
concepts.contentHtml:
The present Temple of the Tooth, Sri Dalada Maligawa, stands beside the old royal palace in Kandy, capital of the last independent Sinhalese kingdom. Vimaladharmasuriya I housed the relic there in the late sixteenth century; the present temple was built by Vira Narendra Sinha in the early eighteenth century, and the last king, Sri Vikrama Rajasinha, added the octagonal pavilion and the moat. In 1815 the Kandyan chiefs ceded the kingdom to Britain at a conference held in the palace's audience hall. The sacred city became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988, and in 1998 a truck bomb attributed to the Tamil Tigers (LTTE) damaged the temple's front.

The tooth itself is kept inside nested caskets in an inner shrine and is very rarely shown; monks make offerings there three times a day. Its great public occasion is the Esala Perahera, held each July or August. For about ten nights, processions of dancers, drummers, torch-bearers and decorated elephants pass through the city, culminating around the full moon and ending with a water-cutting ceremony in the Mahaweli River. A tusker carries a golden casket at the head of the procession, but the casket holds a replica, not the tooth.

The festival joins two older strands: processions for the four guardian deities of Kandy's shrines (Natha, Vishnu, Kataragama and Pattini), linked to prayers for rain, and the tooth procession Faxian saw. By the usual account, King Kirti Sri Rajasinha gave the tooth first place in the eighteenth century, at the urging of monks from Siam who had come to restore the Sri Lankan ordination lineage.

title: Incorruptible Bodies
description: Saints who did not decay, the science of preservation, and Lenin's tomb

concepts.title: What "Incorrupt" Means
concepts.contentHtml:
In Catholic and Orthodox tradition, an incorrupt body is the corpse of a holy person that has failed to decay as expected, sometimes reported with a sweet scent, the "odor of sanctity," or with limbs that stay flexible. Medieval hagiography treated incorruption as a sign that the saint's flesh already shared in the resurrection. Opening the tomb to inspect a candidate's remains became a routine step in the long investigations that precede canonization.

The Church has been more cautious than popular devotion. Prospero Lambertini, later Pope Benedict XIV, in his treatise on beatification and canonization (1734 to 1738), discussed preserved bodies at length and insisted that natural causes be ruled out first; an embalmed body did not count. Today incorruption is neither required for sainthood nor accepted as one of the miracles a cause needs, and Vatican officials have acknowledged that burial conditions can explain slow decay.

Preservation is often partial. At Padua, the tongue and jaw of Saint Anthony (died 1231) are displayed in reliquaries; Saint Bonaventure, who saw the tongue intact when the tomb was opened in 1263, took it as a sign of Anthony's gift for preaching. Devotional catalogs such as Joan Carroll Cruz's The Incorruptibles (1977) list about a hundred cases, but their condition ranges from near-lifelike to dry, darkened mummies, and the label is applied loosely. Orthodox tradition likewise venerates incorrupt relics while distinguishing them, in principle, from ordinary mummification.

concepts.title: Bernadette and the Wax Masks
concepts.contentHtml:
Bernadette Soubirous, the miller's daughter whose visions at Lourdes in 1858 made it one of the world's great pilgrimage sites, became a nun at Nevers and died there on 16 April 1879, aged 35. Her body was exhumed three times during her canonization process. In September 1909 the examiners reported it intact, though her rosary and crucifix had corroded; the body was washed and reburied. In 1919 a doctor described it as practically mummified, with patches of mold and a layer of salts. At the last exhumation, in 1925, relics including two ribs were removed and the body was prepared for display.

The face had darkened and the eyes and nose had sunk, and the community feared that the public would read this as corruption. A thin wax mask was therefore molded, using photographs and an imprint of her face, and fitted over it, with wax coverings for the hands. Since 1925 she has lain in a glass and gilt reliquary in the chapel at Nevers. The masks are openly acknowledged; what visitors see is wax over a preserved but darkened body.

The pattern recurs. Pope John XXIII, exhumed in 2001, was found in good condition; this was attributed to the embalming he received in 1963 and a sealed coffin, and he was displayed with his face lightly covered in wax. Padre Pio, exhumed in 2008, was shown with a lifelike silicone mask. The masks are presented as reverence, a way to show the saint with dignity, not as evidence of a miracle.

concepts.title: Grave Wax, Dry Crypts and Lenin
concepts.contentHtml:
Science offers several mechanisms for bodies that resist decay. In cool, damp, airless graves, body fat can turn into adipocere ("grave wax"), a soapy, crumbly substance formed by the slow breakdown of fats, which can hold a body's shape for centuries. In dry, ventilated crypts the opposite happens: tissue dries out before bacteria can consume it, producing natural mummification. Sealed lead coffins, cold and a lean body all slow decomposition. Italian paleopathologists examining revered bodies have also found evidence of evisceration or embalming that later tradition had forgotten.

The most famous deliberately preserved body is secular. When Vladimir Lenin died on 21 January 1924, the Soviet leadership decided, over the reported objections of his widow, Nadezhda Krupskaya, to keep him on display. The scientists Vladimir Vorobiev and Boris Zbarsky developed the embalming method, and the body has lain on Red Square ever since, from 1930 in Alexey Shchusev's granite mausoleum. It was evacuated to Tyumen in Siberia during the Second World War, shared the tomb with Stalin's body from 1953 to 1961, and is still regularly re-treated in a bath of glycerol and potassium acetate.

The historian Nina Tumarkin, in Lenin Lives! (1983), traced how the Lenin cult echoed the Orthodox veneration of incorrupt saints that the Bolsheviks were attacking at the same moment: between 1918 and 1920 they opened dozens of saints' shrines to show the public the bones and dust inside. Later regimes copied the tomb, preserving Ho Chi Minh, Mao Zedong and Kim Il Sung, though both Ho and Mao had asked to be cremated.

title: The Shroud of Turin
description: A linen cloth, a bishop's complaint, a carbon date, and the business of pilgrimage

concepts.title: Lirey, 1350s: The Shroud Enters the Record
concepts.contentHtml:
The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth about 4.4 meters long and 1.1 meters wide, woven in a herringbone twill and bearing the faint front and back image of a naked man with wounds matching the Gospel accounts of crucifixion. Its documented history begins in the 1350s at Lirey, a village in Champagne, where the knight Geoffroi de Charny had founded a collegiate church in 1353. A lead pilgrim badge found in Paris, now in the Musée de Cluny, shows the cloth displayed above the coats of arms of Charny and his wife, Jeanne de Vergy. There is no secure record of the object before this.

An early document is a memorandum of about 1389 from Pierre d'Arcis, bishop of Troyes, to the Avignon pope Clement VII. D'Arcis complained that the Lirey canons were exhibiting the cloth again to draw offerings, and wrote that his predecessor, Bishop Henri de Poitiers, had investigated it around 1355 and found that it had been "cunningly painted," the truth "attested by the artist who had painted it." Defenders of the shroud point out that the memorandum survives only in unsigned drafts and that no independent record of Henri's inquiry survives.

Clement VII's response, in 1390, was a compromise: exhibitions could continue, provided it was announced that the cloth was a "figure or representation" of Christ's shroud, not the shroud itself. In 1453 Marguerite de Charny passed it to the House of Savoy. It was scorched in a chapel fire at Chambéry in 1532 and patched by Poor Clare nuns, moved to Turin in 1578, and bequeathed to the pope by Umberto II, the exiled last king of Italy, in 1983.

concepts.title: The 1988 Radiocarbon Test
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1898 the amateur photographer Secondo Pia found that his glass negative of the shroud showed a far clearer, lifelike face, and modern scientific interest began. In 1978 a mostly American team, the Shroud of Turin Research Project (STURP), examined the cloth directly. Most of the team concluded that the image was not painted, while the microscopist Walter McCrone, who studied their samples, reported iron-oxide pigment and argued that it was. How the image formed remains disputed.

On 21 April 1988 a strip was cut from one corner of the cloth, divided, and sent to three laboratories, at the University of Arizona, the University of Oxford and ETH Zurich, along with control samples of known age. Cardinal Anastasio Ballestrero of Turin announced the result that October, and the joint paper appeared in Nature in February 1989: the linen dated to 1260 to 1390 CE at 95% confidence. That range falls just before the Lirey exhibitions and the bishop's complaint.

The test has been challenged. In 2005 the chemist Raymond Rogers argued that the sampled corner was a medieval repair rewoven with cotton, but textile specialists who had handled the cloth, including the restorer Mechthild Flury-Lemberg, found no sign of such reweaving. In 2019 a team led by Tristan Casabianca obtained the laboratories' raw data and argued that the measurements were statistically inconsistent, so the published range was less secure than claimed; they did not show a first-century date. None of the laboratories has withdrawn the result, and no new samples have been released for dating since 1988.

concepts.title: Icon, Relic and the Pilgrim Economy
concepts.contentHtml:
The Catholic Church has never officially declared the shroud authentic. Recent popes have set the question aside: John Paul II called it a "mirror of the Gospel," and Francis an "icon" of a man scourged and crucified. That language lets it be honored as an image that leads believers to the Passion, whatever its origin. Its rare public expositions in Turin draw crowds in the millions. A 2018 bloodstain-pattern study by Matteo Borrini and Luigi Garlaschelli concluded that the stains could not all come from one position of a real body, adding to the case for an artistic origin.

The shroud's first documented use, raising offerings for a small church, points to the economy around relics. After the Fourth Crusade looted Constantinople in 1204, Byzantine relics flooded the West. King Louis IX of France bought the Crown of Thorns, which the Latin emperor of Constantinople had pawned to Venetian creditors, for a price usually given as 135,000 livres, and built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris (consecrated 1248) to house it at a cost of about 40,000 livres. The crown was rescued from the Notre-Dame fire of 2019.

Pilgrimage multiplied the trade. At Canterbury, after Thomas Becket's murder in 1170, pilgrims bought tiny flasks of water said to be tinged with his blood and lead badges to pin to their hats, until Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538. Frederick the Wise of Saxony gathered about 19,000 relics at Wittenberg by 1520, with indulgences reckoned at nearly two million years off purgatory. In that same town, in 1517, Martin Luther had issued his Ninety-five Theses against the abuse of indulgences.
